q: Which land animal is pregnant the longest, at about 22 months?
why: An elephant carries its calf for roughly 22 months, nearly two years.

q: Which non-primate has fingerprints so human-like they could confuse detectives?
why: Koalas evolved ridged fingertip patterns remarkably similar to human prints.

q: How many neck vertebrae does a giraffe have?
why: Same as a human; each giraffe neck vertebra can be about 25 cm (10 in) long.

q: Where does a sea otter keep its favourite tool rock?
why: Sea otters store a rock in a loose skin pouch under the foreleg to crack shellfish.

q: Besides the platypus, which mammal lays eggs?
why: Echidnas and the platypus are the only living egg-laying mammals (monotremes).

q: What colour is the fluid hippos secrete that helps protect their skin?
why: Nicknamed 'blood sweat', it is neither blood nor sweat and acts as a sunscreen.

q: About what fraction of all mammal species are bats?
why: With over 1,400 species, bats make up roughly 20% of mammals.

q: How many compartments does a cow's stomach have?
why: The rumen, reticulum, omasum and abomasum let cows digest tough grass.

q: What colour is a polar bear's skin?
why: Black skin absorbs heat; the fur is actually translucent, not white.

q: Which tiny rodent can live over 30 years, remarkable for its size?
why: One captive naked mole-rat lived at least 32 years.

q: About how long is a giraffe's tongue?
why: It is dark purple-black and roughly 45-53 cm (18-21 in) long, handy for stripping thorny leaves.

q: Which big cat cannot roar?
why: Cheetahs chirp and purr instead; their voice box lacks the roaring structure.

q: How many hours a day does a giant panda spend eating?
why: Bamboo is low in nutrition, so pandas spend about 12-14 hours a day eating.

q: Which of these animals physically cannot vomit?
why: A strong valve at the stomach entrance blocks anything coming back up.

q: In Afrikaans, what does 'aardvark' literally mean?
why: Early Dutch settlers in South Africa named it for its burrowing and pig-like snout.

q: If you shaved a tiger, what would you find?
why: A tiger's stripes are in its skin as well as its fur.

q: Which part of a dog is unique to each dog, like a human fingerprint?
why: The ridge pattern on a dog's nose is individual to each animal.

q: Why are beaver incisors orange?
why: Iron in the enamel makes the teeth tougher and gives the orange colour.

q: A newborn kangaroo is about the size of what?
why: It is only about 2 cm long and crawls into the pouch on its own.

q: Which mammal is the only one wholly covered in scales?
why: Pangolin scales are made of keratin, the same material as human fingernails.

q: About how far can a skunk's spray reach?
why: The spray can reach roughly 3-4 m (10-12 ft); the smell travels much further.

q: What changes colour in reindeer between summer and winter?
why: Reindeer eyes shift from golden in summer to blue in winter.

q: Which deer species has antlers on both males and females?
why: Reindeer (caribou) are the only deer where females regularly grow antlers.

q: About how many hours a day does a lion rest?
why: Lions save energy for short bursts of hunting, mostly at dusk and night.

q: Which striped-legged forest animal is the giraffe's only living relative?
why: The okapi of the Congo has zebra-like leg stripes but is a giraffid.

q: In spotted hyena clans, who is in charge?
why: Females are larger and dominant; even low-ranking females outrank immigrant males.

q: What does a camel's hump store?
why: A hump holds tens of kilograms of fat that can be used as energy.

q: A newborn giraffe drops about how far when it is born?
why: Mothers give birth standing up, so calves drop more than 1.5 m (5 ft) to the ground.

q: What are rhino horns made of?
why: Same protein as hair and fingernails; there is no bone core.

q: Which land animal has the largest eyes, about 5 cm across?
why: An ostrich's eye is about 5 cm across, bigger than its brain.

q: Owls can turn their heads by up to about how many degrees?
why: Owls have 14 neck vertebrae (humans have 7) plus blood-vessel adaptations; their eyes are fixed, so they turn the head instead.

q: What gift do some male penguins give to court a mate?
why: Adelie and gentoo males present stones used to build the nest.

q: Which bird has the longest wingspan, up to about 3.5 m?
why: The record wingspan, 3.63 m, belonged to a wandering albatross; it can glide for hours over the ocean.

q: What makes flamingos pink?
why: Carotenoids in algae and small crustaceans colour their feathers.

q: Which bird is the fastest runner, reaching about 70 km/h?
why: It can sprint at about 70 km/h and keep up around 50 km/h.

q: How fast can a peregrine falcon dive?
why: Guinness lists about 320 km/h in a hunting dive; one trained falcon was clocked near 390 km/h.

q: Which bird has been shown to recognise individual human faces?
why: Crows remember people who threatened them and can pass this on to others.

q: Where are a kiwi's nostrils?
a: At the tip of its beak
why: Kiwis sniff out worms in the soil, unique among birds.

q: Pigeons feed their chicks something called what?
why: Both parents make a nutritious secretion in the crop lining.

q: A woodpecker's long tongue wraps around what?
why: In many woodpeckers the bones supporting the tongue loop around the back of the skull.

q: Which flightless bird has a dagger-like claw about 12 cm long?
why: The inner toe claw of a cassowary can reach about 12 cm.

q: Which bird can stay airborne for about ten months without landing?
why: Tracked swifts stayed airborne for almost all of their roughly ten-month non-breeding period; some never landed at all.

q: Which bird migrates from the Arctic to Antarctica and back each year?
why: Tracking found an average round trip of about 71,000 km, the longest known annual migration.

q: Which bird builds the largest nest of any North American bird?
why: The record bald eagle nest, in Florida, was 2.9 m wide, 6 m deep and estimated at over 2 tonnes.

q: Which flightless parrot is the heaviest parrot in the world?
why: It weighs up to about 4 kg and is active at night.

q: How fast can a hummingbird's heart beat per minute?
why: A blue-throated hummingbird's heart has been measured at about 1,260 beats per minute.

q: In emperor penguins, who incubates the egg through the Antarctic winter?
why: He balances it on his feet for about two months without eating.

q: In 2007, T. rex collagen was found to be most similar to which animal's?
why: Proteins from a T. rex bone were closest to those of chickens.

q: A group of owls is called a what?
why: The collective noun nods to the owl's wise reputation.

q: Which bird famously makes hooked tools from twigs and leaves?
why: Wild individuals craft hooked tools to extract insects from wood.

q: Besides eating, what does a toucan's huge beak help it do?
why: Blood flow through the beak lets it shed excess heat, like a radiator.

q: What does a common cuckoo chick do soon after hatching?
why: The blind hatchling heaves the host's eggs out of the nest.

q: Which bird's chicks have claws on their wings for climbing?
why: Young hoatzins use wing claws to scramble through branches and lose them as adults.

q: Many birds can see which type of light that humans cannot?
why: UV vision helps birds spot fruit, mates and insects.

q: Which Australian bird can mimic camera shutters and chainsaws?
why: Superb lyrebirds copy sounds from their surroundings, including man-made noises.

q: Which seabird has been recorded sleeping while flying?
why: Frigatebirds nap in brief bursts mid-flight, sleeping far less than on land.

q: How many hearts does an octopus have?
why: Two pump blood through the gills and one serves the rest of the body.

q: In seahorses, who carries the babies until they are born?
why: The female deposits eggs in the male's brood pouch, where he gives birth.

q: Jellyfish have existed for roughly how long?
why: They predate dinosaurs, and even trees, by hundreds of millions of years.

q: Which jellyfish can revert to a juvenile stage and is called 'immortal'?
why: It can transform its cells back to the polyp stage, restarting its life cycle.

q: A narwhal's 'tusk' is actually what?
why: It is a spiralled tooth that can grow over 2 m long.

q: Which of these has existed the longest on Earth?
why: Sharks date back over 400 million years; the first trees came later.

q: A shark's skeleton is made of what?
why: It is the same flexible tissue found in your nose and ears.

q: Some sharks shed about how many teeth in a lifetime?
why: Some sharks shed around 35,000 teeth, constantly replacing them from rows behind.

q: Which tiny crustacean can punch hard enough to crack aquarium glass?
why: Its club strikes with the acceleration of a small-calibre bullet.

q: The electric eel is not a true eel. What is it?
why: It can discharge more than 600 volts to stun prey.

q: Which fish holds the egg record, with about 300 million in one female?
why: Guinness lists a female sunfish carrying about 300 million eggs; it may have been a bump-head sunfish rather than the common ocean sunfish.

q: Some sea cucumbers breathe by pumping water through what?
why: Water enters the rear and flows into internal 'respiratory trees'.

q: What does a sea star pump through its body to work its tube feet?
why: Its water vascular system pumps seawater to operate hundreds of tube feet.

q: Where are most of an octopus's neurons?
why: About two-thirds of its roughly 500 million neurons are in its arms and body.

q: About how wide is a giant squid's eye, among the largest of any animal?
why: Giant squid eyes can be about 27 cm across, helping it see in deep, dark water.

q: How do dolphins sleep without drowning?
a: One brain half at a time
why: One hemisphere rests while the other keeps them surfacing to breathe.

q: What do bottlenose dolphins use to 'name' each other?
why: Each dolphin develops its own whistle, and others copy it to call that individual.

q: Which mammal holds the deep-dive record, nearly 3,000 m?
why: One tagged individual reached about 2,992 m.

q: Biologically, what is an orca?
why: Orcas are the largest members of the dolphin family.

q: Which reef fish produces sand by eating coral and excreting it?
why: Parrotfish bite off chunks of coral while feeding on algae and grind it into fine sand that they excrete.

q: What hunting trick do humpback whales use with bubbles?
why: They blow a spiral of bubbles to corral fish into a tight ball.

q: Which sea turtle is the deepest diver, reaching over 1,000 m?
why: A leatherback has been recorded at around 1,280 m.

q: In some deep-sea anglerfish, what do tiny males do to females?
why: The male's body merges with the female, who then supplies his blood.

q: Which small reef fish appears to pass the mirror self-recognition test?
why: Researchers reported wrasses trying to remove marks seen only in a mirror.

q: In what position have sperm whales been seen napping?
why: Groups drift motionless, tail down, for about 10 to 15 minutes.

q: How does a sea star feed on a clam?
why: It everts its stomach through the clam's tiny gap and digests it outside.

q: How much honey does one worker bee make in her lifetime?
why: It takes the lifetime work of many bees to fill a single jar.

q: What does a honeybee's waggle dance communicate?
why: The angle shows direction relative to the sun; duration shows distance.

q: Dragonflies catch about what share of the prey they pursue?
why: Studies report dragonflies catching up to 95% of the prey they chase.

q: A headless cockroach can survive for about how long?
why: It breathes through body spiracles and eventually dies of thirst.

q: Which mosquitoes bite people?
why: Females need blood protein to develop their eggs.

q: Butterflies taste with which body part?
why: Taste receptors on their feet tell them if a leaf is good for laying eggs.

q: Periodical cicadas emerge on a cycle of how many years?
why: They spend those years underground as nymphs, then emerge in the millions.

q: Adult mayflies live for about how long?
why: Adults have no functional mouthparts and cannot feed; some live only a few hours.

q: A bombardier beetle defends itself by spraying what?
why: Two chemicals mix in a chamber, reaching close to 100 degrees C.

q: Which insect navigates using the Milky Way?
why: A 2013 study showed dung beetles roll straight under a starry sky.

q: A honeybee's wings beat about how many times per second?
why: That rapid beat produces the characteristic buzz.

q: A ladybird defends itself by releasing foul-tasting fluid from where?
why: This 'reflex bleeding' smells and tastes bad to predators.

q: Which insect group holds the length record, over 60 cm with legs?
why: A Chinese stick insect measured 62.4 cm with legs outstretched, beating the previous record holder, Chan's megastick.

q: A single silkworm cocoon is made from one thread about how long?
why: A silkworm spins one continuous filament that can be up to about 900 m long.

q: Which insect pollinates figs, completing its life cycle inside them?
why: Many fig species rely on their own specific wasp species.

q: What do leafcutter ants do with the leaves they carry?
why: The ants farm fungus on the chewed leaves and eat the fungus.

q: A dragonfly's compound eyes have about how many lenses?
why: Each eye has up to roughly 30,000 facets.

q: What is insect 'blood' called?
why: In most insects it carries little oxygen; air tubes called tracheae deliver oxygen instead.

q: Counting a snowy tree cricket's chirps can estimate what?
why: Dolbear's rule: chirps in 15 seconds plus 40 gives roughly the temperature in Fahrenheit.

q: Where are a cricket's ears?
why: Crickets hear with small membranes on their front legs.

q: Which animals were the first sent into space, in 1947?
why: US scientists flew them on a captured V-2 rocket to study radiation.

q: The UN says a 1 km2 locust swarm eats as much daily as how many people?
why: Swarms can contain tens of millions of insects.

q: What lets a water strider walk on water?
why: Waxy hairs and surface tension keep its legs from breaking the surface.

q: Monarch caterpillars become toxic to predators by eating what?
why: Toxins from milkweed stay in the butterfly into adulthood.

q: How many eyes does a honeybee have?
why: Two large compound eyes plus three simple eyes on top of the head.

q: How do insects breathe?
why: Tiny holes lead to tubes that carry air directly to tissues.

q: In true flies, the hind wings have evolved into what?
why: These tiny balance organs act like gyroscopes during flight.

q: A chameleon's tongue can reach about how many times its body length?
why: Studies found small chameleons can shoot the tongue up to about 2.5 times body length in a fraction of a second.

q: Which large lizard has laid fertile eggs without a male?
why: Zoo females have produced hatchlings by parthenogenesis.

q: What decides the sex of baby alligators?
why: Warmer or cooler nests produce different sexes.

q: Sea turtles find their birth beaches partly using what?
why: Hatchlings imprint on the magnetic signature of their home coast.

q: Jonathan of St Helena, hatched around 1832, is what kind of animal?
why: Guinness lists Jonathan, a Seychelles giant tortoise, as the oldest known chelonian ever.

q: Why do snakes flick their tongues?
why: The tongue carries chemicals to an organ in the roof of the mouth.

q: What covers a snake's eyes instead of eyelids?
why: This 'spectacle' is shed along with the skin.

q: Which snake is the longest in the world?
why: Reticulated pythons can exceed 6 m.

q: What does the king cobra mainly eat?
why: Its scientific name Ophiophagus means 'snake eater'.

q: What are rattlesnake rattles made of?
why: The rattle is made of loosely linked keratin segments, like fingernails.

q: What force lets geckos cling to walls?
why: Millions of tiny foot hairs create weak molecular attractions; some research suggests electrostatic effects also help.

q: What is it called when a lizard drops its tail to escape?
why: The detached tail keeps wriggling to distract the predator.

q: Which lizard can run across water for several metres?
why: It is nicknamed the 'Jesus Christ lizard' for the trick.

q: Which lizard can squirt blood from its eyes?
why: Several horned lizard species can squirt an aimed stream of blood more than a metre to deter predators.

q: A turtle's shell is fused to its what?
why: A turtle cannot leave its shell; it is part of the skeleton.

q: With its mouth closed, which reptile shows its lower teeth?
why: Its lower fourth tooth fits into a groove visible on the outside of the snout.

q: Which reptile, last of its order, lives only in New Zealand?
why: Its lineage dates back to the age of dinosaurs.

q: Chameleons can see about how much of their surroundings?
why: Each eye moves independently.

q: Which land snake has the most toxic venom, by mouse tests?
why: Its venom has the lowest lethal dose in mouse tests of any land snake.

q: A diabetes drug, exenatide, was developed from which lizard's saliva?
why: Its saliva contains a hormone that regulates blood sugar.

q: Which sense do a rattlesnake's heat pits provide?
why: Pits sense body heat from warm prey even in darkness.

q: How do Southeast Asian Draco lizards glide?
why: Elongated ribs unfold into wing-like membranes.

q: How does a marine iguana get rid of excess salt?
why: Special glands near its nose excrete salty fluid.

q: How does a female Burmese python warm her eggs?
why: Muscle shivering raises the temperature of the clutch.

q: How do 'flying snakes' stay aloft?
why: They flatten into a wide shape and undulate.

q: Which body part helps some turtles breathe underwater?
why: Fitzroy River turtles absorb oxygen through the cloaca.

q: Chameleons mainly change colour for what?
why: Colour changes signal mood and help regulate temperature.

q: How does Australia's thorny devil lizard collect water?
why: Tiny grooves in its skin funnel moisture to its mouth.

q: Which giant snake gives birth to live young instead of laying eggs?
why: Females give birth in water to dozens of young.

q: A cheetah's top speed is closest to which figure?
why: The fastest timed cheetah, Sarah, reached about 98 km/h (61 mph) in 2012.

q: Which North American animal can hold about 88 km/h and keep going far longer than a cheetah?
why: Pronghorn can hold about 88 km/h (55 mph) for half a mile and near 72 km/h (45 mph) over much longer distances.

q: A blue whale can weigh about as much as how many African elephants?
why: Blue whales average around 160 tonnes (the heaviest recorded was about 190 tonnes), versus around 6 tonnes for a large African elephant.

q: Which vertebrate may live around 400 years?
why: Eye-lens radiocarbon dating estimated the oldest shark studied at about 392 years, and at least 272.

q: Which is the smallest bird in the world, about 6 cm long?
why: Males weigh about 1.6 grams; it lives only in Cuba.

q: 'Ming', found in 2006, was dated at 507 years old. What was it?
why: Counting growth rings in its shell revealed the age.

q: Which land mammal makes the longest overland migration?
why: Some caribou herds make round-trip migrations of more than 1,200 km a year.

q: Which is the largest living land carnivore?
why: Adult males typically weigh 400-600 kg.

q: Which is the largest living rodent?
why: The largest capybaras weigh around 66 kg.

q: An ostrich egg equals about how many chicken eggs?
why: It weighs about 1.4-1.5 kg, the largest egg of any living bird.

q: Which bird dives deepest, over 500 m?
why: An emperor penguin dive of 564 m is the deepest accurately measured for any bird.

q: Which animal has the largest brain of any, about 8 to 9 kg?
why: Guinness puts it at around 9 kg, about six times a human's.

q: Which animal holds the record for most legs, over 1,300?
why: Eumillipes persephone has 1,306 legs.

q: The largest living reptile can exceed 6 m. Which is it?
why: Big males can weigh over a tonne.

q: Which bird holds the altitude record, hit by a plane at about 11,300 m?
why: The collision happened over Ivory Coast in 1973.

q: Which is the world's heaviest spider?
why: It can weigh up to about 175 g, with a leg span up to about 30 cm.

q: Which mammal can live over 200 years?
why: Eye-lens chemistry suggested one bowhead was about 211 years old; old harpoon points found in others pointed to ages over 100.

q: Which animal has the strongest bite force ever measured?
why: A 2012 study measured about 16,460 newtons, the greatest bite force directly measured in a living animal.

q: Which is the largest living primate?
why: Male eastern lowland gorillas can weigh up to about 210 kg.

q: Which is the heaviest known invertebrate?
why: One specimen caught in 2007 weighed about 495 kg.

q: A blue whale calf gains about how much weight a day?
why: Calves gain around 90 kg a day in their first year, living only on mother's milk.

q: Which mammal has had the largest recorded litter, over 30 young?
why: Guinness records a wild litter of 31.

q: Which is the heaviest snake?
why: The heaviest reliably weighed specimen was about 97.5 kg; claims of far heavier ones are unverified.

q: The largest amphibian ever recorded, about 1.8 m long, was what kind of animal?
why: The 1.8 m record specimen is now thought to belong to the South China giant salamander, recognised as a separate species in 2019.

q: Which lizard is the heaviest in the world?
why: Large wild adults weigh around 70 kg.

q: What shape are wombat droppings?
why: Their intestines shape them into cubes, so they stay put on rocks and logs.

q: What colour is an octopus's blood?
why: It uses copper-based hemocyanin rather than iron-based hemoglobin.

q: What do frogs pull down to help push food down their throat?
why: Retracting the eyes presses food toward the throat.

q: A garden snail can have roughly how many tiny teeth?
why: The average garden snail has around 14,000 microscopic teeth on a ribbon-like tongue called a radula.

q: Why do some storks and vultures excrete on their own legs?
why: Evaporation cools the blood flowing through the legs.

q: A hagfish defends itself by releasing what?
why: The slime can clog the gills of a predator.

q: Which taste can cats not detect?
why: Cats lack a functional sweet-taste receptor.

q: How often does a sloth typically descend to the ground to poop?
why: Three-toed sloths climb down roughly once a week to poop at the base of a tree.

q: What do male platypuses have on their hind legs that females lack?
why: The venom causes severe pain in humans.

q: Which salamander can regrow limbs, its spinal cord and parts of its brain?
why: Scientists study it to understand regeneration.

q: Scientists have located penguin colonies from space by spotting what?
why: Guano stains the ice a visible reddish-brown in satellite images.

q: What is a baby echidna or platypus called?
why: Both are monotremes and hatch from leathery eggs.

q: Rabbits re-eat special soft droppings called what?
why: This lets them extract nutrients missed the first time.

q: What do rats make when tickled, according to researchers?
why: Researchers likened the chirps to rat laughter.

q: What do zebra stripes best help deter, according to studies?
why: Horseflies struggle to land on striped surfaces.

q: Vampire bats will share blood meals with whom?
why: They regurgitate blood to feed starving roostmates, even unrelated ones.

q: Which tiny animal has survived the vacuum of open space?
why: Tardigrades survived exposure on a 2007 European mission.

q: Which North American frog survives with much of its body frozen solid?
why: Up to around 65% of its body water can freeze.

q: Koalas sleep about how many hours a day?
why: Eucalyptus leaves give little energy, so koalas conserve it.

q: Which stinging insect do elephants avoid so much that farmers guard crops with hives?
why: Elephants flee the sound of angry bees.

q: How do flamingos position their heads to feed?
why: They filter food from water with their beaks turned upside down.

q: A fungus called Ophiocordyceps forces infected ants to do what?
why: The fungus then grows from the ant's body.

q: A group of flamingos is called a what?
why: A fitting name for such colourful birds.

q: A group of ravens is poetically called what?
why: Unkindness is a traditional collective noun for ravens.

q: What shape are the pupils of goats and sheep?
why: They give a wide view to spot predators.

q: Hippos spend hours in water but cannot do what?
why: Too dense to float, they push off the bottom and bounce along.

q: A pistol shrimp stuns prey by snapping its claw to create what?
why: The bubble's collapse makes a loud shockwave.
